title: A click replaces state

blocks.md:
## Next state is a new value

React state is replaced, not edited in place. A click computes the next value and hands it back. `click(count)` should return `count + 1` without changing the argument. The old number stays what it was. The new number is a different value that will be stored next, then the screen redraws from that replacement.

This bites when you write `count++` or assign back into `count` and return the same box you were given. Mutation is easy to miss, and later code that still holds the old variable can see a surprise. Returning a fresh number makes the update obvious and keeps the previous count honest.

```javascript
function click(count) {
  return count + 1;
}
console.log(click(0)); // 1
console.log(click(1)); // 2
```

A common mistake is returning the original `count` unchanged, or mutating a shared object. The exercise asks you to return the next count so the prints are `1` then `2`.
